newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea to ship corn to North, seek to reopen talks.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea to ship corn to North, seek to reopen talks.

text.p: The South Korean Red Cross said on Monday it would begin delivering 15,000 tonnes of corn to North Korea next week to help stave off famine and seek the resumption of talks with its Northern counterpart.
Lee Byung-woong, secretary general of the South Korean Red Cross, said his organisation planned to give its North Korean counterpart an estimate of how much other food aid was planned.

That issue had created a deadlock in inter-Korean Red Cross talks in Beijing aimed at speeding up aid shipments. The talks, held earlier this month, were the first contact between the two Korean organisations in nearly five years.
The North demanded to know the exact amount of aid before it would discuss how the grain would be delivered.
A statement from the South Korean organisation said 3,600 tonnes of corn would be sent to the North next week to begin the delivery by train of 15,000 tonnes of corn bought in China.
"It is difficult to secure train cars to load the corn but donors are working hard to send all of them as soon as possible," an organisation spokesman said.
The corn was donated by dozens of local religious and civic groups that have set a target of raising enough funds to buy another 95,000 tonnes of corn in the next two months.
Lee on Monday met representatives from those groups and others to ask them how much more they could contribute.
He said the South Korean Red Cross, the only window for private-sector aid to the communist North, would compile the answers and pass the information on to Pyongyang.
"We would like to compile all commitments in a week to 10 days and inform the North," Lee told Reuters. "I would like to see the resumption of South-North Red Cross talks this month."
International aid groups have said North Korea, hit by devastating floods in 1995 and 1996, is sliding into famine, with the hungry eating bark, leaves and mushroom stems.
Last week, North Korea slammed South Korea for the deadlock at the Beijing talks, calling the failure to give the amount of aid "eccentric and incomprehensible attitude."

Lee, the chief South Korean delegate in the Beijing talks, said his delegation could not tell Northern delegates the amount of assistance at the time as it would depend on how much South Korean citizens were willing to donate.
Lee said on Monday he expected civic groups to commit well over $10 million in view of initial responses from them.
Soh Kyung-suk, representative of the Korean Sharing Movement that coordinates corn supply to the North, accused the Seoul government of not fully supporting their campaign.
"The government says there has been no national consensus over the issue of aid to the North but the government has not even organised a forum to discuss the matter," he said.

Lee said his organisation wanted to speed up delivery of relief supplies by setting up channels for directly handing over aid rather than using the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies as a go-between as in the past.
"The months of May, June, July and August will probably be the most difficult months for North Koreans," Lee said, adding that the harvest would begin in September.
